newsitem.title: FINLAND: Clinton wins through on NATO trouble at summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wins through on NATO trouble at summit.

text.p: The United States and Russia agreed at their summit to tone down the bitter row over NATO enlargement in spite of their disagreements, but the meeting seemed to represent a clear victory for Western interests.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who can be expected to portray the summit as a triumph in front of his communist and nationalist critics at home, made two important concessions.

Firstly, he committed himself in Helsinki to cutting out the tough anti-NATO rhetoric that has worried governments across Central and Eastern Europe by promising with Clinton to "minimise the consequences of this disagreement".

Secondly, Yeltsin formally dropped Moscow's demand that a new charter being negotiated between NATO and Russia should be legally binding, accepting instead that it would be signed by NATO leaders and therefore be politically binding.

In return, Clinton promised to continue work on the charter, repeated some existing NATO assurances on the deployment of troops and nuclear weapons and then firmly pledged that enlargement would go ahead on schedule.
Eastern European countries, worried that Russia could force a deal that would leave them out in the cold, welcomed this reassurance from the United States.

While Clinton was careful not to appear triumphant, Polish President Alexander Kwasniewski -- whose country expects to be among the first invited to join NATO at an alliance summit in July -- put it more bluntly in Warsaw.
"I think that in this basic question...Russia has agreed on the expansion of NATO," he said.
Yeltsin, of course, did not do so in public and in fact registered his continued disapproval of the alliance's plans, which Moscow says will threaten Russia's security.
"We believe that the expansion of NATO is a mistake and a serious one at that," he said.
Yeltsin also denied suggestions at the news conference that the West was buying off Russia with economic help.

But there was no more talk of retargeting nuclear missiles or changing Russian foreign policy to forge new links with countries like China and Iran. Whether the calm lasts is, of course, another matter.

Moreover, Clinton said the new NATO-Russia charter would give Moscow a "voice but not a veto" in European security and that new members of the alliance would not in any sense be "second class citizens" enjoying less protection than others.

Russia had been pushing for all sorts of legally-binding commitments on NATO deployments and a promise that former Soviet republics, particularly the Baltics, would never be admitted to the alliance. Yeltsin got none of this in Helsinki.
